Most teams blame model behavior, but in practice the failure is broken loops. Here is the 5-loop runbook: tests, research, implementation, PR maintenance, and /goal.
Save this checklist if you want Claude Code to finish work, not just write code.
 
The shift
The old workflow was simple:
You think. You write code. You run tests. You read errors. You patch. You repeat.
The new workflow is different:
You define the goal. You give Claude the right tools. You set boundaries. Claude runs the feedback loop. You review the result.
That does not remove the developer.
It moves the developer up a level.
You are no longer only the person typing the code. You are the person designing the system that gets the code finished.
That is a much bigger change than autocomplete.
Autocomplete helps you write the next line.
Loops help you close the work.
What a loop is
A loop is the cycle Claude Code runs when it has a task and tools.
The Agent SDK docs describe the loop in plain terms. Claude receives a prompt, evaluates what to do, calls tools, receives tool results, and repeats until it produces a final response. [E1]
That sounds abstract, so here is the practical version.
You ask Claude to fix failing tests.
It runs the test command. It reads the failure. It opens the relevant files. It edits the bug. It runs the test again. It sees a new failure. It patches again. It verifies the result. It tells you what changed.
That is the agent loop.
The important part is not that Claude writes code.
The important part is that Claude can stay inside the feedback cycle long enough to produce a verified result.
This is why Claude Code feels different from normal chat.
Chat gives you an answer.
A loop works through state.
Why developers should care
Software development is full of loops.
A bug fix is a loop.
Reproduce the bug. Find the cause. Patch the cause. Run the test. Repeat until it holds.
A feature is a loop.
Understand the existing pattern. Implement the smallest change. Run the local checks. Fix integration breaks. Repeat until the acceptance criteria hold.
A pull request is a loop.
Open PR. Wait for CI. Read the failure. Patch the branch. Address review comments. Repeat until it is mergeable.
A deployment is a loop.
Ship. Watch logs. Check health. Handle rollback signals. Confirm the rollout.
The old developer carried those loops manually.
Claude Code can now carry more of them.
That means your bottleneck changes.
The bottleneck is no longer, "Can I type this implementation fast enough?"
The bottleneck becomes, "Did I define the loop clearly enough that the agent can make progress safely?"
The new developer skill
The junior version of AI coding is:
 
The senior version is:
 
That second prompt is not longer because the developer likes ceremony.
It is longer because it defines a loop.
It tells Claude:
where to look
what success means
how to verify
what not to touch
when to stop
when to ask for help
That is the new craft.
The best developers will not be the people who ask for code.
Everyone can ask for code.
The best developers will be the people who turn messy work into reliable loops.
Five loops worth learning
You do not need a complicated agent framework to start.
Start with five loop types.
Use this table as the quick map:
 
1. The test-fix loop
Use this when you have a failing test or broken build.
Prompt:
 
This loop works because the test is an objective judge.
Claude does not need to guess whether it succeeded. The command exits clean or it does not.
This is the safest place to give an agent autonomy.
2. The research loop
Use this when you do not understand a codebase yet.
Prompt:
 
This loop is read-only.
It is perfect for onboarding, unfamiliar repos, and risky systems where editing too early would cause damage.
A good research loop ends with a map, not a diff.
3. The implementation loop
Use this when you have a clear feature and known acceptance criteria.
Prompt:
 
This is where most developers should spend their time.
The key is to make the acceptance criteria concrete.
Bad:
"Improve the dashboard."
Good:
"Add a compact launch checklist panel to the dashboard. It must fit inside the existing 100vh layout, avoid page-level scrolling, persist state in local storage, and pass the dashboard build."
The second version gives the loop rails.
4. The PR maintenance loop
Use this when a branch is waiting on CI or review.
Prompt:
 
This is where scheduled loops become useful.
Claude Code's scheduled task docs say /loop can rerun a prompt automatically while the session stays open. You can give it a fixed interval or let Claude choose the next interval dynamically. [E2]
Example:
 
or:
 
That turns waiting time into agent time.

You stop babysitting GitHub.
Claude can poll the queue and report or propose fixes, with push and merge still gated by you.
5. The goal loop
Use this when the end state matters more than the interval.
Claude Code has /goal, which sets a completion condition. After each turn, a small evaluator checks whether the condition is met. If not, Claude starts another turn.
Example:
/goal all tests in test/auth pass and npm run lint exits 0, or stop after 12 turns
The distinction matters.
/loop runs because time passed.
/goal runs because the condition is not satisfied yet.
Use /loop for waiting.
Use /goal for finishing.
The loop stack
The most reliable Claude Code setup has four layers.
Layer 1: Instructions
Put durable project rules in CLAUDE.md.
Examples:
 
These rules reduce repeated steering.
They also survive longer sessions better than one-off prompt instructions.
Layer 2: Skills
Skills turn repeated workflows into reusable behavior.
A code review skill can define what to check.
A debugging skill can force reproduce -> isolate -> hypothesize -> verify.
A deploy skill can run the same checklist every release.
Skills are the instinct layer.
They tell Claude how your team works before the task even starts.
Layer 3: Hooks
Hooks make some rules automatic.
Claude Code's hooks reference lists events like PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolBatch, Stop, SubagentStart, and PreCompact. Hooks can block tools, run checks, add context, and trigger commands at specific points in the lifecycle.
Examples:
block destructive shell commands
run a formatter after edits
run tests after specific files change
log tool usage
archive transcripts before compaction
prevent protected files from being edited
A skill asks Claude to behave.
A hook enforces behavior.
You want both.
Layer 4: Loops
Loops keep work moving.
Use the normal agent loop for one task.
Use /loop for recurring checks.
Use /goal for completion conditions.
Use CI and tests as the outside judge.
This is the full pattern:
 
That is the modern AI development stack.
The systems model is simple:
 
A loop optimizes whatever signal you give it. If the signal is only "lint passes," do not expect product correctness.
Think in oracles:
OracleExampleRiskStrongdeterministic test for specified behaviorsafest autonomyWeaklint, snapshots, vague review commentscan pass while intent failsDangerousagent self-evaluation onlyeasy to reward-hack
The agent can verify against commands. The developer still validates that the command represents the real requirement.
How to write better loop prompts
A good loop prompt has six parts.
1. Start state
Tell Claude where to begin.
Start by reading src/billing/service.ts and the nearest tests.
2. Work objective
Define the outcome.
Add coupon validation before checkout session creation.
3. Constraints
Name the boundaries.
Do not change database schema.
Do not touch unrelated checkout code.
Do not add dependencies.
4. Verification
Tell Claude how to prove success.
Run pnpm test billing and pnpm typecheck.
5. Stop condition
Prevent runaway work.
Stop after 3 failed attempts on the same error.
6. Report format
Make the result reviewable.
End with files changed, commands run, pass/fail status, and remaining risks.
Make the report concrete:
 
Here is the full template:
 
Save this.
Most bad Claude Code sessions fail because one of those six parts is missing.
Bad loops vs good loops
Bad loop:
 
Why it fails:
no scope
no success condition
no stop rule
no verification command
no definition of "improve"
Good loop:
 
Why it works:
one module
one bug
test-first proof
bounded scope
clear stop rule
The agent is not magically smarter.
The loop is better designed.
Where loops go wrong
Loops fail in predictable ways.
The goal is too vague
"Make this production-ready" is not a goal.
It is a swamp.
Use concrete checks instead:
 
The feedback is too slow
If every verification run takes 20 minutes, the loop becomes expensive and brittle.
Give Claude the smallest useful check first.
Run one test file before the full suite.
Run typecheck before the full build.
Run a local script before waiting on CI.
The permissions are too broad
Do not give a loop write access to everything by default.
Start read-only.
Then allow edits.
Then allow commands.
Then allow recurring execution.
Autonomy should expand only as verification improves.
The loop has no stop rule
Every serious loop needs a stop condition.
Examples:
 
A stop rule is not weakness.
It is how you prevent the agent from turning uncertainty into churn.
What changed for developers
Claude Code does not make engineering judgment less important.
It makes judgment more visible.
A weak developer says:
"AI wrote it, ship it."
A strong developer asks:
Did the agent inspect the right context?
Did it change the smallest surface area?
Did the verification test the claim?
Did the loop stop at the right time?
Does the diff make the system easier or harder to reason about?
What failure mode would this miss?
The job moves from typing every line to controlling the execution system.
That means architecture matters more.
Tests matter more.
Small interfaces matter more.
Readable errors matter more.
Good repo hygiene matters more.
Agents reward codebases with tight feedback.
They punish codebases where nobody knows how to verify anything.
The practical setup I recommend
If you are starting from zero, do this in order.
Step 1: Write a project CLAUDE.md
Include:
package manager
test commands
build commands
protected files
coding conventions
review expectations
what "done" means
Keep it short.
Rules Claude can remember beat rules nobody reads.
Step 2: Create one debugging skill
Make it force this sequence:
reproduce -> isolate -> hypothesize -> patch -> verify
This prevents the classic AI failure mode:
guess -> edit -> guess again -> create a second bug
Step 3: Add one safety hook
Start with a PreToolUse hook that blocks dangerous commands.
Block things like force pushes, recursive deletes, and commands that read secrets.
Step 4: Add one fast test command
Give Claude a command that runs in under 2 minutes.
If your only test command takes 30 minutes, your agent loop will be painful.
Step 5: Use /goal for one bounded task
Example:
 
Do not start with a giant refactor.
Start with one module and one check.
Step 6: Use /loop for waiting work
Example:
 
Once that works, let it address review comments.
Then let it patch CI failures.
Earn autonomy one loop at a time.
The operator checklist
Before you hand work to Claude Code, ask:
What is the exact end state?
What command proves it?
What files are in scope?
What files are off limits?
How many failed attempts are acceptable?
What should Claude do if the plan changes?
What should the final report include?
If you cannot answer those questions, you are not ready to run the loop.
You are asking the agent to discover the task, define success, execute the work, and grade itself.
That is too much.
Give it a job.
Give it a judge.
Then let it work.
The real lesson
The next era of development is not "AI writes code while humans disappear."
That is the lazy version. The real shift is this:
Humans define outcomes.
Agents run loops.
Tests provide feedback.
Hooks enforce boundaries.
Developers review and ship.
That is the workflow now.
The developer who wins is not the one with the cleverest prompt.
It is the one with the cleanest loop.
If you could instrument one dev bottleneck this week, which one would you turn into a Claude Code loop first?
